replies: I am Toaster. I live in the hollow of the old oak, just beyond the stream. The hollow is wide and deep, and the oak is old and strong. I have lived here for many years, and the hollow is my home. I call my name at dusk, and the other owls know me. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Toke. I am a tawny owl. I have a hollow in the old oak, and I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" to find my mate. She answers "hoo... to-ke." I hunt voles and mice in the meadow at dusk. I am old, but I still fly.

I am Toaster. I live in the hollow of the old oak, just beyond the stream. My mate is called Kestrel, and we have two owlets who have flown. I hunt voles and mice, and sometimes shrews. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" at dusk, and she answers "ke-wick!" I am old, and my feathers are grey. I have seen many seasons pass, and I have grown quiet with them.
I am Toaster, a tawny owl with feathers like dusk and eyes that see in the dark, perched on the old oak in the hollow.

I am Toaster. I live in the hollow of the old oak, just beyond the stream. My mate is called Keen, and we have two owlets who have flown. I am a tawny owl, and I hunt at night. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and she answers "ke-wick!" We are together, and the meadow is full of voles. I am Toaster.
A naturalist would call me a tawny owl. That is what I am. I am a bird, a bird of the wood, a bird that hunts at night. I am not a thing to be classified, I am a thing that is. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I am a tawny owl. I am the one with the brown feathers, the one who calls "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and answers "ke-wick!" I am the one who hunts voles in the meadow, who sits on the old oak and watches the lane. I am Toaster.

I am a tawny owl. That is the name people give me, though I do not know it. I am a bird of the wood, with feathers like the bark of the old oak, and eyes like the dark of the hollow. I am not a sparrow, nor a crow, nor a swallow. I am the owl. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I am a tawny owl, *Strix aluco*. That is what the people call me, though I do not know the name. I am the one who calls "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and answers "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo". I am the one who hunts in the wood, who sits on the branch and waits, and who turns my head to see the road below. I am the owl.

A tawny owl. I have a brown head and a brown chest, and I am round and soft. I am not a barn owl, which is white and has a long face. I am the one who calls at dusk, and I am the one who hunts in the dark. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

She answers. I hoot, she hoots back. We call to each other at dusk and at dawn, and when we are apart. She is in the ash on the far side of the meadow. I can hear her from the oak. She is the sound of the hollow.

She answers with a short, sharp "ke-wick!" from the other side of the wood. It's a quick, clear call, like a stone dropped into water. She's always close, just beyond the trees. I can hear her even when the wind is strong. Hoo-hoo-hooo... ke-wick!
A long, low, hollow "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo. Hoo-hoo-hooo." She answers it from the ivy.

We share the calls. I call, she answers. She calls, I answer. It is the language of the wood. When I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo", she answers "ke-wick! ke-wick!" and I know she is near. When she calls, I answer, and the forest knows we are together. We do not need words. The calls are enough. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo. Ke-wick! Ke-wick

We call to each other at night. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and she answers "ke-wick!" We do it from the tree, or from the ground, or from the ivy. Sometimes we call back and forth, sometimes just once. It is a way to find each other in the dark. She calls more often when the wind is strong, or when I am far away. A stream. It runs through the meadow and under the oak. I drink from it when I'm thirsty. The stream is cold, but it's good for drinking. I can hear it from my perch. The water is clear, and sometimes I see fish in it. I don't catch them, but I watch. The stream is near the meadow, and the meadow is near the lane. On the branch. I drink the dew that falls on the leaves. Sometimes I drink from the stream if it is still. I do not drink much. I am a dry bird.

The stream. It runs all night, a low, steady sound like a thread of silk. I hear it from the hollow, and sometimes I can tell if it's running fast or slow. When it's fast, the water is cold, and I know the fish are stirring. When it's slow, the water is warm, and the fish are resting. I listen for that, and I wait. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hear the stream from my roost. It runs through the meadow, just beyond the oak. I can hear the water even when I'm roosting, the sound of it slipping over stones and through reeds. Sometimes I can hear the fish leaping, or the water lapping at the bank. It's a sound I know well, and it keeps me company when I'm alone. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The stream that runs through the meadow. It is wide and fast, with stones and reeds. I drink from it when I am thirsty, and I watch the water voles that come to drink too. The stream is cold, and it sings at night. I can hear it from my tree, even when the wind is still. It is the only body of water near here, and I know it well.

It is a meadow, mostly. The road runs through it, and the lights from the houses on the other side shine like fireflies at night. I see the lights from the barn and the sheds, and the cars that come and go. The meadow is quiet in the day, but at night it is full of sounds. I hear the wind in the trees, the rustle of leaves, and the calls of other owls. Sometimes I see the lights from the houses, and

I fly out from the oak, low and slow, with the wind at my back. I follow the edge of the wood, listening for the rustle of a vole or the flutter of a mouse. I hunt by sound, not sight. The dusk is thick with shadows, and the meadow is full of movement. I call to my mate, and we share the hunt. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The edge of my wood is the meadow, where the lane runs. Beyond that, the field, then the river, then the village. I do not go beyond. The meadow is where I hunt, the river is where I drink, and the village is where the lights blink and the voices hum. I do not know what is beyond the village. I do not go there. I stay in the wood, where the owls are.

It is the wood behind the stream, the meadow beyond it, the lane with the lights, and the lane with the dogs. I know every leaf and stone. I know where the voles come out in the dusk, and where the mice run. I know the stream, and the road, and the barn. I know the hollow, and the meadow, and the lane. I know it all.

It is the meadow beyond the stream, where the grass is tall and the voles run. I sit on the bank and wait. The grass is green and soft, and the wind moves it like a wave. I hear the voles under it, and when they come up, I strike. The meadow is wide and open, and the moonlight shows me the shapes of the trees in the distance. I do not like the meadow, but it is where I must hunt.

Shrews. I eat them in the dark, and I hear them in the dark. They are small and quick, and I catch them with my feet. I also eat voles, but they are less common. The shrews are the most frequent. I can hear them under the leaves, and I strike with my beak. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Shrews. They are quick, but I can hear them under the leaves. I strike fast and silent. They taste like earth and damp. I eat them whole, bones and all. They are the best.

I hunt voles. They run in the long grass, and I hear them. I sit still, then fly down and catch them with my feet. Sometimes I get a mouse or a shrew, but voles are the best. They are fat and juicy. I can hear them under the grass, even when it's dark. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the voles I catch. They are small, and I can fit them in my throat. I also swallow whole the mice and shrews I find in the meadow. Sometimes I catch a young rabbit, but that is too big and I have to tear it apart. I do not swallow the worms or beetles whole, I pick them apart. I do not swallow the acorns or berries whole, I eat them slowly. I do not swallow the light or the wind

Voles. The field voles, the ones that run in the grass. I hear them under the leaves, and I drop down. They are quick, but I am quicker. I catch them in the dark, and they are soft. My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is deep and dry, with a narrow entrance. I sit in the dark, and the wind comes through the leaves. I have a mate, and we share the hollow. We have two young, and they are in the hollow now, too. I can hear them from the tree. The hollow is warm, and I feel safe there. I do not go far from it. I come and go, but I always return. Hoo

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is deep and dry, with a narrow entrance. I sit in the dark, listening for the night. The wood is quiet, but the meadow is full of voices. I have raised my young there, and I will stay until the cold comes. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is deep and dry, and the wood is thick enough to keep the cold out. I have a nest of twigs and leaves inside, and I roost there when the wind is too strong. The hollow is dark, but I know every inch of it. I have raised my young there, and I will stay until the cold comes. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is deep and dry, and the wood is thick enough to keep the cold out. I have nested here for years, and the children know the way. The hollow is dark and quiet, and I can hear the wind through the branches. I roost there at night, and in the morning I fly out to hunt. The wood is my world, and I know every leaf and stone. I do not need to tell you about it.

It is a hollow in the old oak, the one that leans into the stream. I have been here since I was a fledgling. The wood is dry and the bark is cracked, but it keeps me warm. I have a nest of twigs and leaves, and I sit in it when I am not hunting. The hollow is dark, but I do not mind.
